The small Bleeker Street shops were stocked with goods from other folksy artists, either designing beatnick clothing, African ethnic jewelry or middle eastern patchwork home furnishings, including mirrored pillows and bongo drums. The Look was changing from sleek 50's post modern to a new Look called WHATEVER .....as long as it shakes and sparkles. Today in 2015 at 71, both my age numbers and myself have reversed. I have returned once again to live near Bleeker St but in the the East Village. After spending 45 years in the posh upper east side on E 63rd St making custom gowns for VIP's at Bergdorf Goodman, I once again am wandering the streets that so inspired me at 17. I prefer the East side as my beloved Cafe Figaro is now an ice cream chain. I stay today in NYC with my dear Parsons classmate artist, Mary Alice Orito, who was just named President of NAWA, the oldest association of women artists. In 1961 Mary Alice worked at Margaret Moore on 8th st selling hippy chic jewelry, while a block away from my brownstone my hippy-home-brick walled shop. The artists and folk singers I met in the cafés bought my clothes, especially my black or forrest green skin tight leather pants.

title: Only English Speakers Capitalize 'I,' But That Doesn't Mean We're Obsessed With Ourselves
article_500: English is the only language that capitalizes first-person singular nominative pronouns. In German, all nouns are honored with capitalization. Spanish speakers talk about themselves using "yo," and, Russian speakers write a small "я" In the Middle Ages, it was easy for a little "i" to get lost on the page in a sea of lowercase letters and scribes began elongating "i," like a lowercase "j" without the dot when it appeared at the end of a word, a linguistics professor says."I" will remain the widespread rule forever. But for now, English speakers, you can save your energy for the real grammar issues at hand, like comma usage and single spacing. "Note that only 'I' is capitalized [in English], and not 'me,' 'my,' 'mine,' 'we,' 'us,' 'our,'" Paul Kiparsky pointed out. "It's like saying Germans may be more materialistic because they capitalize all noun's," professor Adele Goldberg of Princeton University said. "I don’t think anyone would entertain either claim," she said. 'I" is the first person pronoun of the ﬁrst person in English, while in some other languages it is the second person that is honoured by this distinction, Otto Jespersen wrote more than 100 years ago. The real story behind the great capital "I," according to Jes Persen, is an "innocent one"

Title: Only English Speakers Capitalize 'I,' But That Doesn't Mean We're Obsessed With Ourselves
=========================

Did you know that only English speakers have to capitalize the letter "I"? That's right! In English, we write "I" with a capital letter, while in other languages, it's the second person that gets the special treatment. This might make some people think that we're obsessed with ourselves, but that's not true!

The reason we capitalize "I" is because it's the first person singular nominative pronoun in English. In the past, it was easy for a little "i" to get lost on the page, so scribes started making it look like a lowercase "j" without the dot. Today, we still do this to help our words stand out.

Other languages have their own ways of showing respect for pronouns. For example, in German, all nouns are capitalized, while in Spanish, we say "yo" and in Russian, we write a small "я". So, even though we might be the only ones who capitalize "I", it's not because we're obsessed with ourselves.

So, the next time you see someone writing "I", remember that it's just a special way of showing that it's talking about the person who is reading or writing the sentence. And don't worry about capitalizing other words, like "me" or "my", because those are just regular words that don't need any special treatment.

title: On the Holiness of Plastic: Interviewing Dorothea Lasky
article_500: Dorothea Lasky was my very first poetry professor at Columbia, where I'm studying for my MFA. A month into our time together, I told Dottie I wasn't writing frequently enough, that I felt tense and was overthinking when I went to write. Her response was to send me a text message every night for the entire month of October, 2013. Every night I turned somersaults, guzzled a rainbow of different fruit juices, plunged into scalding baths--all the while jotting down phrases on a big yellow legal pad. The end of every ritual culminated in a poem. As time passed, a sense of the spiritual and sacred suffused my apartment and all of its contents. It had all become part of my poetry--the thing that mattered most to me in the world. The night after I completed the Ninth Universe, I wrote a Tenth. More Universes followed and eventually, with her earlier prompts, they formed the bedrock of my first chapbook, AEONS, winner of the 2014 Poetry Society of America Chapbook competition. It's a rare thing for a book of poems to be born in a single classroom. I wanted her to discuss her educational philosophy, which is idiosyncratic in the extreme. Do you think you need to learn all about someone before you can help them make art? What is the link between intimacy and teaching--teaching poetry or anything else? And how would you have taught me if we didn't have so much in common?

The cost of producing a single object or an edition is determined based in part on what the foundry is asked to do -- make molds, build a supporting structure, cast the piece, patinate, install the finished work, transport and store molds and insure the molds. The first thing that sculptors should ask for is a quote that is in the range of a change of order, because alterations are likely to be made during the design or fabrication process. Rubens' art should be understood as an alchemic manipulation of something dead (pigments) into something alive (Inmortal Art). Besides, while Velazquez used to be a painter of peace (his war paintings depict people at rest), Rubens is a painterof violence. There is always blood in his paintings to the point that it is not far fetched to think that he uses blood, when he paints, as an allegor of painting for the end of the day, when there is nothing else to paint. That is the RA's less than precise approach to art history. So Rubens invented the rainbow, apparently, apparently. title: Pika's Moss-Eating Habit May Help Creature Adapt To Climate Change Rather Than Succumb To It
article_500: Pikas living in rockslides near sea level in Oregon survive hot temperatures by eating more moss than any other mammal. Researchers observed 220 hours of pika behavior and were surprised to find that the animals were eating so much moss. Pikas are very sensitive to heat, and the tiny critters can die if they spend more than two hours above 78 degrees Fahrenheit. Living at a lower elevation with warmer temperatures gives the animals access to what the biologists describe as a "year-round salad bar""Mosses are 80 percent fiber. It's a bit like eating paper," said Denise Dearing, senior author of the study. "To our knowledge, this study represents the highest degree of voluntary moss consumption reported for a mammalian herbivore in the wild," said Jo Varner, a biology doctoral student at the University of Utah. "Few herbivores consume moss because it's so nutritionally deficient. The pikas in our study actually set a new record for moss in a mammal's diet: 60 percent," said Dearing. "Some fiber is good, but this is almost all fiber," said the study's senior author. "It's the bit of paper that you eat when you're trying to survive in the winter," Dearing said of the moss-eating pik as a source of fiber for the animals. The study was published in the February 2014 issue of the Journal of Mammalogy, which is published by the American Museum of Natural History and Science.

title: Apple quietly retires one of its Apple Music tiers
article_500: Apple is retiring its Voice plan for Apple Music that lets people use Siri to select tracks for $5 a month. The tech giant introduced its most affordable Apple Music plan in 2021 but on Wednesday said ina message on its websitethat it’s ending the ability to sign up to it with immediate effect. Current subscribers to Voice can use the service until the end of their billing period. The auto-renew function has been turned off. Apple is encouraging those on the Voice plan to switch either Individual, Student, or Family, or to consider signing up for Apple One, a bundle that includes Apple Music, Apple TV+, and more. It's not clear why Apple is retiring Voice, but it's possible the take-up wasn’t as great as it had hoped. The Siri-powered Voice tier was useful for those who mainly listened to music in their car or on a HomePod where they just called out tracks, with a library or visual interface being of little importance.

Sea levels rose by 17 cm last century and the rate has accelerated to more than 3 mm a year. U.N. panel of scientists says heat-trapping gases from burning fossil fuels are nudging up temperatures. A small number of scientists dismiss human-influenced global warming, arguing natural climate fluctuations are responsible for sea-level rise.. Some scientific studies have projected sea level rise of up to 2 metres by 2100, a figure that would swamp large. tracts of land from Bangladesh to Florida. The IPCC has said temperatures are likely to be 0.4 to 1.0 degrees Celsius warmer from 2016-35 than in the two decades to 2005. The Ice2sea project has said sea levels would rise by between 16.5 and 69 cm under a scenario of moderate global warming this century. The biggest impact rising seas will have is that storms will be more destructive in the near future, says David Vaughan, head of the Ice2Sea project. The project is trying to narrow down uncertainties about how melting ice will swell the oceans. It is based on a study by the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, a leading climate research institute in Germany. The study is the first to examine evidence from climate history and combine it with computer simulations of contributing factors to long-term sea- level increases. "Our results indicate that major adaptation at our coastlines will be necessary," says Anders Levermann.

title: Night Parrot, Nocturnal Bird In Australia, Seen Alive For First Time In Over A Century
article_500: A nocturnal Australian parrot that had not been seen alive for more than a century has not only been seen but has been photographed. Scientists had previously based their knowledge of the critically endangered Night Parrot on the occasional dead specimen. "The strangest thing about this parrot, living on the ground, it hops like a little kangaroo," said John Young, a naturalist. Young's alleged sighting on May 25 in the northern state of Queensland was the culmination of a 15-year quest to find the parrot. The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) listed the bird as critically endangered in 2012, its population depleted by feral cats, foxes and changes in the environment after European settlement in Australia. "In the time I had with the bird the other night, it is the most sensitive bird I have ever seen," said Young, who is keeping the location of the sighting a secret. "For now, keeping the locality a secret is the way to go," said CSIRO's Leo Joseph, the director and research leader of the wildlife collection at government research body CSIRO. "I think the worst thing we can do at the moment is to let too many people anywhere near it," he said. The parrot is small with yellowish green plumage, mottled with brown and black specks. It hides in spinefex grass during the day and is active at night, hiding in the undergrowth in Queensland's northern Queensland state.

title: In the Shit With Thoreau: A Walden for the Anthropocene

The defining environmental challenge is climate change. Climate change means there is no "wild" place, nowhere that human beings have not changed. The environmentalism that was defined by wildness/wilderness has drawn criticism for being elite, mainly white, male-centered, nostalgic from the start, and indifferent to most of the adult and workaday world. It turns out, too, that an Anthropocene ThOREau is more than wishful thinking. It is a lot of baby to toss out with the pre-Anthropocene bathwater. It was John Muir, the founder of the Sierra Club and a giant publicist of giant, wild landscapes, who switched Thoreaux's "wildness" to literal wilderness. He was hopelessly tied to trackless, depopulated places - the kinds of places he hardly saw or wrote about during a lifetime in New England. Turns out that wilderness isn't in his works as he works as his new new friend, as he does with his bean-field, he writes. It's a new era in Earth's history: the Anthropocene, the age when humanity becomes a force in the planet's development. It means we have take responsibility for a world we partly create, says Julian Zelizer, a professor at the University of California, Los Angeles.

What We Can Learn:
=========================

* Resilience: The people of Glasgow have shown resilience by setting up a music trust after a tragic event.
* Creativity: The trust helps young people develop their creativity through music and the arts.

How can we be more like the people of Glasgow and use our creativity to help others heal and grow?
